ns_smoke.name: Rising Smoke Plume
ns_smoke.question: How does buoyancy turn a smooth column into a turbulent plume?

layers.title: The question
layers.text: How does buoyancy turn a smooth column into a turbulent plume?

layers.title: What the colours and motion show
layers.text: A source of buoyant, dyed fluid at the floor. The column rises, shears against the still air, rolls up into vortices and entrains its surroundings.

layers.title: One change to try
items: Set the vorticity confinement to 0 to see how much of the small-scale detail is added by that model term.

layers.title: What to measure
layers.text: The plume-rise diagnostic and the kinetic energy growth.
more: Halve the buoyancy coefficient and compare the plume-rise curve.

layers.title: Physical explanation
layers.text:
Heat a parcel of fluid and it expands, becomes less dense than its surroundings, and is pushed upward by buoyancy — Archimedes' principle in a moving fluid. A continuous hot source therefore drives a rising column. As the column rises it drags still fluid along its edges; the velocity difference creates shear, the shear rolls up into vortices, and those vortices entrain surrounding fluid and tangle into the turbulent, billowing structure we call a plume.

Mathematically this is the incompressible Navier–Stokes system: conservation of momentum for a fluid whose density is treated as constant except in the buoyancy term (the Boussinesq approximation). The flow must also satisfy incompressibility, ∇·u = 0 — locally as much fluid leaves a point as enters it. That single constraint is what makes incompressible flow hard: the pressure is not a thermodynamic variable here but a Lagrange multiplier that instantly adjusts everywhere to keep the velocity divergence-free.

The same equations and solver govern visual-effects smoke, the dispersion of pollutants and volcanic plumes, and ventilation and fire modelling in buildings.

layers.title: Equations, symbols and assumptions
layers.text:
• u — the fluid velocity field
• ∂t u + (u·∇)u — acceleration of a fluid parcel (local + convective)
• −∇p — the pressure-gradient force that enforces incompressibility
• ν∇²u — viscous diffusion of momentum (friction)
• f_b — the buoyancy body force, proportional to temperature/dye
• ∇·u = 0 — incompressibility: the velocity field has no sources or sinks

layers.title: Initial and boundary conditions (this preset)
layers.ic: Quiescent ambient fluid with no dye; the source switches on at t = 0.
layers.bc: No-penetration (free-slip) floor carrying a hot, dyed source patch; free-slip side walls; open (zero-gradient) top so the plume can leave the domain.

layers.title: Numerical method, checks and limitations
layers.text: A projection ('stable fluids') method: unconditionally-stable semi-Lagrangian advection, a red-black Gauss–Seidel SOR solve of the pressure-Poisson equation to enforce ∇·u = 0, a Boussinesq buoyancy force proportional to the transported temperature/dye, and vorticity confinement that re-injects the fine swirls numerical diffusion erodes.
layers.checks: Qualitative demonstration: the projection method keeps the flow divergence-free to the solver tolerance; vorticity confinement is a visual modelling term, not a physical property.

layers.title: References
items: Fedkiw, R., Stam, J. & Jensen, H.W. (2001). Visual simulation of smoke. SIGGRAPH 01 (vorticity confinement).

buoyancy.label: Buoyancy coefficient
buoyancy.help: Buoyancy coefficient: force per unit of the transported scalar (dye/temperature). Higher → a faster, more vigorous plume.

confinement.label: Vorticity confinement
confinement.help: Vorticity confinement — re-injects small-scale swirl lost to numerical diffusion (a modelling knob, not a physical property). 0 = none.

viscosity.label: Viscosity
viscosity.help: Kinematic viscosity ν — how 'thick' the fluid is. Lower → finer, more chaotic structures; higher → smoother, damped flow.

flicker.label: Source flicker
flicker.help: Wobble & pulse the source (a prescribed modulation of the inflow, not a physical instability). 0 = a steady column; 1 = a lively, flame-like pulse.

source.label: Source width
source.help: Width of the hot source at the floor.

resolution.label: Resolution
resolution.help: Grid resolution. It changes the grid, and with it whatever a scene ties to the grid: the elapsed convective time in the wind tunnel, the Rayleigh number in the convection scenes, the grain size in the rock, the extent of the blast box. The derived readouts say what moved for this experiment; runs at different resolutions are comparable only where they say so.

duration.label: Duration (×)
duration.help: Simulated interval as a multiple of the scene's reference interval (1.0 = default).
